note:
Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 72-year-old male here about rough spots on your scalp and face. Who came with you today?
Family member: I'm his daughter. I drive him to his appointments and set up his pill box, so I'll fill in what he forgets.
Patient: She remembers things better than I do.
Doctor: That helps. Tell me about the spots.
Patient: I've got scaly, rough patches on top of my head and on my forehead. They've been there about two years, but lately a few of them are crusty and sore when I comb my hair.
Family member: He worked outdoors as a landscaper for forty years and never wore a hat. One spot on his left temple bled last month after he scratched it.
Doctor: Has any spot grown quickly, or is there an open sore that won't heal?
Patient: The one on my temple looks bigger than it used to. Nothing is oozing now.
Doctor: Any itching?
Patient: Some itching, yes.
Doctor: Any fever, weight loss, or new lumps in your neck?
Patient: No fever, no weight loss, and I haven't felt any lumps.
Doctor: Have you ever had skin cancer, or tried any treatment on these spots?
Patient: A basal cell cancer was cut off my nose about ten years ago.
Family member: And he used fluorouracil cream last winter, but he stopped it after two weeks because his face got raw and red.
Patient: Yes, it burned too much, so I quit.
Doctor: Understood. Now please go through your medicines with me.
Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg every morning and amlodipine 5 mg once a day for my blood pressure, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, aspirin 81 mg daily, and metformin 500 mg twice a day for the sugar.
Family member: Dad, that's not right. The metformin was raised to 1000 mg twice a day in the spring. The 500 mg tablets are the old ones.
Patient: Oh, that's right. It's 1000 mg twice a day now.
Doctor: Good, so metformin 1000 mg twice a day. Your primary doctor sent recent labs for your diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol. Your A1c was 7.2, and creatinine was 1.3 with an eGFR of 54. Let me examine you now. Your blood pressure today is 138/80. There are multiple pink, rough, scaly papules across the scalp and forehead, about eight in total, each three to six millimeters. The lesion on the left temple is eight millimeters, thicker and crusted, without ulceration. I don't feel any enlarged lymph nodes in your neck, and there is no new pigmented lesion.
Doctor: This is actinic keratosis from many years of sun exposure. The thick spot on the left temple concerns me for an early squamous cell carcinoma, so I want a shave biopsy of that one today. The others I'll treat now with liquid nitrogen cryotherapy. It will sting and may blister.
Family member: Should he restart the cream?
Doctor: Not the fluorouracil, since it irritated him. Once the frozen areas heal, I'll start imiquimod 3.75% cream once daily at bedtime to the scalp and forehead for two weeks, then two weeks off, then repeat. Keep taking your other medicines, including the aspirin, as you are now. Use sunscreen SPF 50 every morning and a wide-brimmed hat. Come back in four weeks to review the biopsy and do a full skin check, and call us sooner if a spot bleeds, grows, or becomes painful.
Patient: Okay, we'll do that.
Family member: I'll write it all down.
summary: A 72-year-old male came to dermatology with his daughter for rough, scaly patches on the scalp and forehead present for about two years, with a left temple spot that has enlarged and bled. He denied fever and weight loss, had stopped fluorouracil cream because of irritation, and had a basal cell cancer removed years ago. Examination showed multiple scaly papules and a thicker crusted 8 mm left temple lesion without ulceration or enlarged neck nodes. The assessment was actinic keratosis, with concern for early squamous cell carcinoma at the temple. The plan was a shave biopsy, cryotherapy, later imiquimod cream, sun protection, and a four-week follow-up.

soap.subjective: 72-year-old male with rough, scaly patches on the scalp and forehead for about two years; some are crusty, sore, and itchy, and a left temple spot looks bigger and bled last month. He denies fever, weight loss, and neck lumps, and nothing is oozing now. His daughter, who attends and helps with history, reports 40 years of outdoor landscaping work without a hat. History: basal cell cancer cut off the nose about ten years ago, diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol. Fluorouracil cream last winter was stopped after two weeks because his face became raw and red. Medications: lisinopril 20 mg every morning, amlodipine 5 mg once a day, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, aspirin 81 mg daily, and metformin 1000 mg twice a day (he first said 500 mg; his daughter corrected him that it was raised to 1000 mg in the spring).
soap.objective: BP 138/80. Recent labs from the primary doctor: A1c 7.2, creatinine 1.3, eGFR 54. About eight pink, rough, scaly papules of 3 to 6 mm on the scalp and forehead. Left temple lesion 8 mm, thicker and crusted, without ulceration. No enlarged lymph nodes in the neck and no new pigmented lesion.
soap.assessment: Actinic keratosis from long-term sun exposure. The thick left temple lesion raises concern for early squamous cell carcinoma, pending biopsy.
plan: Shave biopsy of the left temple lesion today
Liquid nitrogen cryotherapy to the other lesions today
After the treated areas heal, start imiquimod 3.75% cream once daily at bedtime to the scalp and forehead for two weeks, two weeks off, then repeat
Do not restart fluorouracil cream because it caused irritation
Continue other medications as currently taken, including aspirin
Sunscreen SPF 50 every morning and a wide-brimmed hat
Return in four weeks to review the biopsy and do a full skin check; call sooner if a spot bleeds, grows, or becomes painful

note:
Hospital day 2. 45-year-old male admitted to the medical ward with sepsis from a urinary source.

Overnight: Fever to 38.9 C early in the admission has resolved. No rigors overnight and no hypotension. He reports less flank pain today and dysuria is improving. He denies nausea, vomiting, or confusion. No bleeding noted on anticoagulation.

Current medications: ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (day 2). Apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, continued at the same dose.

Vitals: Temp 37.6 C, HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air.

Exam: Alert and oriented, comfortable. Mild right CVA tenderness. Abdomen soft and nontender, no suprapubic pain. No peripheral edema.

Data: WBC 15.2, down from 19.8. Creatinine 1.0. Lactate has cleared to 1.4 from 3.1. Hemoglobin stable at 14.1. Urine culture is growing E. coli, and one of two blood cultures is positive for the same organism, susceptibilities pending. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis.

Sepsis due to urinary tract infection: improving. Continue ceftriaxone and narrow once susceptibilities return. Repeat CBC and basic metabolic panel in the morning. Plan to transition to an oral antibiotic in 24 to 48 hours if he remains afebrile and stable.

Atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation: rate controlled, no bleeding. Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Monitor hemoglobin.
summary: A 45-year-old male on hospital day 2 is being treated for sepsis from a urinary source and takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. His fever has resolved, flank pain and dysuria are improving, and he has no bleeding. Labs show a falling white count and cleared lactate, urine and blood cultures are growing E. coli, and renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis. The plan is to continue ceftriaxone, narrow by susceptibilities, and continue apixaban at the same dose, with transition to an oral antibiotic in 24 to 48 hours if he stays stable.

soap.subjective: Hospital day 2 for a 45-year-old male with sepsis from a urinary source. Fever to 38.9 C early in the admission has resolved; no rigors or hypotension overnight. He reports less flank pain and improving dysuria, and denies nausea, vomiting, confusion, or bleeding. He takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation and is on ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily.
soap.objective: Temp 37.6 C, HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. Alert, comfortable, mild right CVA tenderness, abdomen soft and nontender without suprapubic pain, no peripheral edema. WBC 15.2 (down from 19.8), creatinine 1.0, lactate 1.4 (from 3.1), hemoglobin 14.1. Urine culture growing E. coli; one of two blood cultures positive for the same organism, susceptibilities pending. Renal ultrasound without hydronephrosis.
soap.assessment: Sepsis due to urinary tract infection, improving. Atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, rate controlled with no bleeding.
plan: Continue ceftriaxone and narrow once susceptibilities return
Repeat CBC and basic metabolic panel in the morning
Transition to an oral antibiotic in 24 to 48 hours if afebrile and stable
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily and monitor hemoglobin

note:
31-year-old female, ED, rheum consulted by phone
CC: R great toe pain x 1 day

HPI: Woke at 3 AM w/ severe throbbing pain R great toe, can't tolerate the sheet touching it. Peak pain 9/10. Mild swelling and redness. 1st episode. Denies fever, chills, trauma, recent illness, other joint pain, rash. Denies hx kidney stones. No hx GI bleed or ulcer.
PMH: HTN x 2 yr, obesity (BMI 34).
FH: father w/ gout.
Meds: HCTZ 25 mg daily. Takes no NSAIDs at home. NKDA.
OTC supplements: niacin 500 mg daily x 6 mo "for cholesterol", creatine 5 g daily, tart cherry gummies.
SH: 2-3 beers + fructose soda most weekends. No tobacco.

Vitals: Temp 37.4 C, HR 96, BP 146/92, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA.
Exam: Uncomfortable, otherwise NAD. R 1st MTP erythematous, warm, swollen, exquisitely TTP, ROM limited by pain. No other joint effusion. No tophi. No rash. Skin intact, no cellulitis streaking. Heart RRR, lungs CTAB.

Results: uric acid 9.1, WBC 11.8, Cr 0.9, CRP 38. UPT neg. XR R foot: soft tissue swelling at 1st MTP, no erosions, no fracture.

MDM: Acute gout flare R 1st MTP, likely precipitated by HCTZ + niacin + alcohol. Septic arthritis less likely (afebrile, typical presentation); no aspiration done. Rheum agrees w/ tx and outpt urate-lowering after flare resolves.

ED tx: colchicine 1.2 mg PO x1 then 0.6 mg 1 hr later. Naproxen 500 mg PO x1 w/ food. Pain 8/10 -> 4/10 on reassessment.

Dispo: d/c home.
- colchicine 0.6 mg BID x 7 d
- naproxen 500 mg BID w/ food x 5 d
- stop HCTZ, start amlodipine 5 mg daily, BP recheck w/ PCP in 1 wk
- stop niacin and creatine
- limit beer + fructose soda, hydrate well
- no allopurinol now; f/u rheum in 2-4 wks to start urate-lowering tx once flare resolved, repeat uric acid then
- return to ED if fever, spreading redness, worsening pain, black stools
summary: A 31-year-old female presented to the ED with one day of severe right great toe pain with swelling and redness, her first such episode. She has hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide and takes over-the-counter niacin, creatine, and tart cherry gummies. Uric acid was 9.1 with a mildly raised white count and a foot x-ray without erosions or fracture. The diagnosis was an acute gout flare of the right first MTP, likely precipitated by HCTZ, niacin, and alcohol. She received colchicine and naproxen and was discharged with HCTZ and niacin stopped, amlodipine started, and rheumatology follow-up.

soap.subjective: 31-year-old female with 1 day of severe throbbing right great toe pain, peak 9/10, with mild swelling and redness; first episode. She denies fever, chills, trauma, recent illness, other joint pain, and rash, with no history of kidney stones or GI bleed. PMH: hypertension for 2 years and obesity (BMI 34); father has gout. Medications: HCTZ 25 mg daily, no NSAIDs at home, NKDA. OTC supplements: niacin 500 mg daily for 6 months, creatine 5 g daily, tart cherry gummies. Drinks 2-3 beers and fructose soda most weekends.
soap.objective: Temp 37.4 C, HR 96, BP 146/92, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air. Uncomfortable; right first MTP erythematous, warm, swollen, exquisitely tender with pain-limited ROM; no other joint effusion, no tophi, no rash, no cellulitis streaking. Heart and lungs normal. Uric acid 9.1, WBC 11.8, Cr 0.9, CRP 38, UPT negative. Right foot x-ray: soft tissue swelling at the first MTP, no erosions or fracture. Pain 8/10 improving to 4/10 after ED treatment.
soap.assessment: Acute gout flare of the right first MTP, likely precipitated by HCTZ, niacin, and alcohol. Septic arthritis considered less likely (afebrile, typical presentation). Hypertension and obesity.
plan: Colchicine 1.2 mg PO then 0.6 mg 1 hour later in the ED, then colchicine 0.6 mg BID for 7 days
Naproxen 500 mg once in the ED, then 500 mg BID with food for 5 days
Stop HCTZ and start amlodipine 5 mg daily; BP recheck with PCP in 1 week
Stop niacin and creatine
Limit beer and fructose soda and hydrate well
No allopurinol now; rheumatology follow-up in 2-4 weeks to start urate-lowering therapy once the flare resolves, with repeat uric acid
Return to the ED for fever, spreading redness, worsening pain, or black stools
Discharge home

note:
Hospital day 2, ICU. 63-year-old male admitted after a syncopal episode at home, with sinus pauses on telemetry.

Overnight: No further syncope. Telemetry showed two pauses of up to 3.9 seconds during sleep, asymptomatic, with sinus bradycardia in the 40s. This morning he denies chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, or headache. No focal weakness.

Medications: Metoprolol tartrate 50 mg twice daily for hypertension was held on admission and remains held.

Vitals: HR 48, BP 132/76, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 36.8 C. Orthostatic vitals negative.

Exam: Comfortable and alert. Slow regular rhythm, no murmur. Lungs clear. Neurologic exam nonfocal.

Data: ECG shows sinus bradycardia at 46 with first-degree AV block and no ST changes. Troponin negative x2. Potassium 4.2, sodium 140, creatinine 1.0, hemoglobin 13.8, TSH 2.1. CT head without acute findings. Echocardiogram: EF 58%, no significant valvular disease.

Syncope: Likely bradyarrhythmic from sinus node dysfunction with beta blocker effect. Continue holding metoprolol. Continue ICU telemetry. Cardiology electrophysiology consulted regarding pacemaker evaluation.

Hypertension: BP acceptable off metoprolol. Monitor.
summary: A 63-year-old male on ICU day 2 was admitted after a syncopal episode, with sinus pauses up to 3.9 seconds and sinus bradycardia on telemetry. He denies chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, and headache, and orthostatic vitals, troponin, CT head, and echocardiogram were unremarkable. The ECG shows sinus bradycardia with first-degree AV block. The syncope is attributed to sinus node dysfunction with beta blocker effect, so metoprolol remains held, ICU telemetry continues, and electrophysiology is consulted about a pacemaker.

soap.subjective: Hospital day 2 in the ICU for a 63-year-old male admitted after a syncopal episode at home with sinus pauses on telemetry. Overnight there was no further syncope, and he had two asymptomatic pauses up to 3.9 seconds during sleep. He denies chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, headache, and focal weakness. Metoprolol tartrate 50 mg twice daily for hypertension was held on admission.
soap.objective: HR 48, BP 132/76, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 36.8 C; orthostatic vitals negative. Comfortable and alert, slow regular rhythm without murmur, lungs clear, neurologic exam nonfocal. ECG: sinus bradycardia at 46 with first-degree AV block, no ST changes. Troponin negative x2, potassium 4.2, sodium 140, creatinine 1.0, hemoglobin 13.8, TSH 2.1. CT head without acute findings. Echocardiogram EF 58% without significant valvular disease.
soap.assessment: Syncope, likely bradyarrhythmic from sinus node dysfunction with beta blocker effect. Sinus bradycardia with first-degree AV block. Hypertension, acceptable off metoprolol.
plan: Continue holding metoprolol
Continue ICU telemetry
Cardiology electrophysiology consulted for pacemaker evaluation
Monitor blood pressure off metoprolol

note: This is an endocrinology consult dictation on the ward for a 68-year-old female admitted three days ago with pneumonia, seen today because a CT of the chest done on admission incidentally showed a right thyroid nodule. She has no prior thyroid history. She denies neck pain, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, or weight loss. Her voice is normal. She has had no neck radiation. Family history is negative for thyroid cancer. Past medical history is hypertension on lisinopril 10 mg daily. She also takes a biotin supplement, 5000 micrograms daily, for her hair and nails. Current inpatient medications are ceftriaxone 1 gram IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg daily, day three, and she is improving with her cough lessening and no fever for 24 hours. Vitals this morning blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 84, correction, heart rate 78 on recheck, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius. On exam she is comfortable. There is a firm right lobe thyroid nodule that moves with swallowing, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no tracheal deviation, and the rest of the gland is not enlarged. No tremor and reflexes are normal. Data: thyroid ultrasound done yesterday showed a solid hypoechoic nodule in the right lobe measuring 2.4 centimeters, correction, 2.6 centimeters in greatest dimension, with microcalcifications, TI-RADS 5, and no suspicious cervical lymph nodes. TSH 1.1, free T4 1.2, calcium 9.3, creatinine 0.9. My assessment is a right thyroid nodule with suspicious sonographic features in a biochemically euthyroid patient, pneumonia that is improving, and stable hypertension. Plan is an ultrasound guided fine needle aspiration of the right nodule tomorrow before discharge. Stop the biotin supplement because it can interfere with thyroid assays, hold it for at least three days, and repeat the TSH and free T4 afterward. Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily. Continue ceftriaxone and azithromycin per the primary team. If the cytology is suspicious or malignant, refer to endocrine surgery. Follow up in endocrine clinic in two weeks. Discussed with the patient and she understands the plan.
summary: A 68-year-old female admitted with pneumonia was seen by endocrinology for a right thyroid nodule found incidentally on chest CT. She has no compressive or hyperthyroid symptoms and is biochemically euthyroid with a normal TSH and free T4. Ultrasound shows a 2.6 cm solid hypoechoic right nodule with microcalcifications, TI-RADS 5, without suspicious lymph nodes. The plan is ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration before discharge, stopping biotin and repeating thyroid tests after three days, and endocrine clinic follow-up in two weeks.

She denies neck pain, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, and weight loss, and her voice is normal. Family history is negative for thyroid cancer. Inpatient ceftriaxone 1 gram IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg daily, day three, with cough lessening and no fever for 24 hours.

Firm right lobe thyroid nodule that moves with swallowing; no cervical lymphadenopathy, no tracheal deviation, rest of the gland not enlarged; no tremor, normal reflexes. Thyroid ultrasound: solid hypoechoic right lobe nodule 2.6 centimeters in greatest dimension with microcalcifications, TI-RADS 5, no suspicious cervical lymph nodes. TSH 1.1, free T4 1.2, calcium 9.3, creatinine 0.9.

Stop the biotin supplement, hold for at least three days, then repeat TSH and free T4
Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily
Continue ceftriaxone and azithromycin per the primary team
Refer to endocrine surgery if cytology is suspicious or malignant
Follow up in endocrine clinic in two weeks

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I'm seeing you after your lab draw this morning. You're a 39-year-old female on chemotherapy for breast cancer, correct?
Patient: Yes, I had cycle three of doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide ten days ago.
Doctor: And I understand you just traveled. Tell me about that.
Patient: I flew home from an overseas trip five days ago. It was a long flight, about fourteen hours, and I stayed with relatives. I know I wasn't supposed to go, but it was a family emergency.
Doctor: How have you been feeling since you got back?
Patient: Tired, really tired, and I've had a mild sore throat for the last two days. My mouth feels sore too.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever. I checked this morning and it was 36.8. No chills either.
Doctor: Any cough, shortness of breath, diarrhea, or burning when you urinate?
Patient: No cough, no shortness of breath, and no burning. I had loose stools once while I was abroad, but it passed in a day.
Doctor: Any sick contacts on the flight or at your relatives' house?
Patient: My cousin had a cold, but nobody was seriously sick.
Doctor: Did you start any new medicines or supplements?
Patient: No, just my usual anti-nausea pills, ondansetron 8 mg. I take it as needed, maybe once a day since chemo.
Doctor: Okay. Your labs this morning show a white blood cell count of 1.4 and an absolute neutrophil count of 0.6, so you're neutropenic. Your hemoglobin is 10.8 and platelets are 142. Your temperature today is 36.9, blood pressure 118/74, heart rate 88, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Let me look. Your throat is mildly red with no white patches, and I see a few small mouth sores on the inside of your cheeks. Your lungs are clear and your abdomen is soft. There's no redness around your port site.
Patient: That's good.
Doctor: This is chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, and the travel adds some infection risk, so we need to be careful. I'm going to delay your next cycle by one week. I want to start filgrastim 480 mcg injected under the skin once a day until your neutrophil count recovers. My nurse will teach you to give the injection. We'll repeat your blood count in two days.
Patient: What should I do at home?
Doctor: Check your temperature twice a day. If it reaches 38 or higher, which is 100.4 Fahrenheit, go to the emergency department right away, don't wait. Avoid crowds and sick contacts, wash your hands often, and rinse with salt water for the mouth sores. Stay away from raw salads and undercooked meat for now.
Patient: Okay. Should I keep taking the ondansetron?
Doctor: Yes, continue ondansetron 8 mg as needed. We'll see you in two days for labs and a recheck. Please call sooner if you develop diarrhea, cough, or chills.
Patient: Thank you.
summary: A 39-year-old female with breast cancer on doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide returned from overseas travel five days ago and presented with fatigue, mild sore throat, and mouth soreness but no fever. Labs showed a white count of 1.4 and an absolute neutrophil count of 0.6, and she was afebrile with a few mouth sores on exam. The assessment was chemotherapy-induced neutropenia with added infection risk from travel. The plan was to delay the next cycle by one week, start filgrastim 480 mcg daily, repeat the blood count in two days, and review fever precautions.

soap.subjective: 39-year-old female with breast cancer, ten days after cycle three of doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide, who flew home from an overseas trip five days ago. She is very tired with a mild sore throat for two days and a sore mouth. She denies fever (36.8 this morning), chills, cough, shortness of breath, and burning with urination, with loose stools once while abroad that passed in a day. A cousin had a cold. Her only other medication is ondansetron 8 mg as needed, about once a day.
soap.objective: White blood cell count 1.4, absolute neutrophil count 0.6, hemoglobin 10.8, platelets 142. Temperature 36.9, blood pressure 118/74, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Throat mildly red without white patches, a few small mouth sores on the inner cheeks, lungs clear, abdomen soft, no redness around the port site.
soap.assessment: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia with added infection risk from recent international travel.
plan: Delay the next chemotherapy cycle by one week
Start filgrastim 480 mcg subcutaneously once a day until the neutrophil count recovers; nurse to teach injection
Repeat blood count and recheck in two days
Check temperature twice a day and go to the emergency department right away for a temperature of 38 or higher (100.4 Fahrenheit)
Avoid crowds and sick contacts, wash hands often, salt water rinses for mouth sores, avoid raw salads and undercooked meat
Continue ondansetron 8 mg as needed
Call sooner for diarrhea, cough, or chills

note:
Pulmonology clinic follow-up for pulmonary embolism. The patient is a 78-year-old female seen for reassessment while on anticoagulation. She lives alone and came to the visit by herself using a volunteer ride service.

History. She first reported that her pulmonary embolism occurred about six months ago, but the hospital discharge paperwork she brought shows it was diagnosed three months ago, and that timeline is the one used here. At that time she presented with sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath after a long car ride, and a CT pulmonary angiogram showed bilateral lower lobe segmental emboli. She completed apixaban 10 mg twice daily for seven days and then stepped down to 5 mg twice daily, which she continues. Today she reports that her exertional dyspnea is much improved, but she still gets winded climbing one flight of stairs. She denies chest pain, hemoptysis, syncope, calf pain, or leg swelling. She has had no epistaxis, melena, or hematuria.

Past medical history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and osteoarthritis of both knees. Her current medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, vitamin D3 1000 units daily, and apixaban. When asked about pain medicines she first said she takes ibuprofen occasionally, but after reviewing the bottles she brought she clarified that it is naproxen 220 mg, one tablet twice daily, taken almost every day for knee pain. She has no known drug allergies.

Social history is important here. She is widowed and lives alone in a second floor apartment, with no family nearby and only a neighbor who checks on her weekly. She no longer drives and has missed appointments when rides fell through. She fills her own weekly pill box and admits missing about three evening apixaban doses over the past month.

On examination, BP was 154/88 and 148/84 on repeat, HR 76, RR 16, SpO2 95% on room air at rest, and weight 68 kg. She was in no distress. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated, rhythm was regular, the lungs were clear without wheeze, and there was no edema. Calves were symmetric and nontender. A 6-minute walk test covered 280 meters with a nadir SpO2 of 92%. The V/Q scan at three months shows near-complete resolution of the perfusion defects with a small residual defect in the right lower lobe. Echocardiogram shows normal right ventricular size and function, estimated RVSP 32 mmHg, and LVEF 60%. Labs show hemoglobin 12.1, creatinine 1.2, and eGFR 48.

Impression: Pulmonary embolism three months ago with good clinical and imaging improvement. There is no evidence of pulmonary hypertension on echocardiogram, and her residual exertional dyspnea is likely related to deconditioning. Her hypertension is above goal, and daily naproxen with apixaban in the setting of CKD adds bleeding and kidney risk.

Recommendations: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily for at least three more months, then reassess for extended therapy at a reduced dose. Discontinue naproxen today and replace it with acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed. Increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily. Request pharmacy blister packaging and a phone alarm for apixaban doses. Refer to social work and home health nursing for medication management and transportation support, and refer to pulmonary rehabilitation. Return in three months, sooner for new chest pain, worsening breathlessness, or any bleeding.
summary: A 78-year-old female who lives alone returned to pulmonology three months after a pulmonary embolism, with improved exertional dyspnea and no bleeding or recurrent symptoms. She had missed some apixaban doses and was found to be taking naproxen daily for knee pain. V/Q scan shows near-complete resolution and echocardiogram shows normal right ventricular function, so the residual dyspnea is attributed to deconditioning. Her blood pressure was above goal. The plan is to continue apixaban, stop naproxen in favor of acetaminophen, increase amlodipine to 10 mg, and add pharmacy packaging, social work, home health, and pulmonary rehabilitation.

soap.subjective: 78-year-old female seen three months after a pulmonary embolism (diagnosed three months ago per discharge paperwork, although she first said six months). It presented with pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath after a long car ride, with bilateral segmental emboli on CT pulmonary angiogram. She took apixaban 10 mg twice daily for seven days, then 5 mg twice daily. Exertional dyspnea is much improved but she gets winded on one flight of stairs; she denies chest pain, hemoptysis, syncope, calf pain, leg swelling, epistaxis, melena, and hematuria. PMH: hypertension, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease stage 3, osteoarthritis of both knees. Medications: amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, vitamin D3 1000 units daily, apixaban, and naproxen 220 mg twice daily almost every day for knee pain (she first said ibuprofen). No known drug allergies. Widowed, lives alone with a neighbor checking weekly, no longer drives, and missed about three evening apixaban doses in the past month.
soap.objective: BP 154/88 and 148/84 on repeat, HR 76, RR 16, SpO2 95% on room air at rest, weight 68 kg. No distress, JVP not elevated, regular rhythm, lungs clear without wheeze, no edema, calves symmetric and nontender. 6-minute walk 280 meters with nadir SpO2 92%. V/Q scan at three months: near-complete resolution of perfusion defects with a small residual right lower lobe defect. Echocardiogram: normal right ventricular size and function, RVSP 32 mmHg, LVEF 60%. Hemoglobin 12.1, creatinine 1.2, eGFR 48.
soap.assessment: Pulmonary embolism three months ago with good clinical and imaging improvement and no evidence of pulmonary hypertension; residual exertional dyspnea likely related to deconditioning. Hypertension above goal. Daily naproxen with apixaban in CKD adds bleeding and kidney risk.
plan: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily for at least three more months, then reassess for extended therapy at a reduced dose
Discontinue naproxen today and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed
Increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily
Pharmacy blister packaging and a phone alarm for apixaban doses
Refer to social work and home health nursing for medication management and transportation support

Doctor: Hello, thanks for coming in. I have you here as a 41-year-old female, referred after an emergency visit for a fast, irregular heartbeat. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. It started racing and fluttering and wouldn't stop, so I went to the ER last week.
Doctor: What did they tell you?
Patient: They said I have atrial fibrillation. They gave me a pill, metoprolol succinate 25 mg, and sent me home.
Doctor: When did the palpitations first start?
Patient: About two weeks ago, I think. Actually no, it was more like two months ago, because I remember feeling it before our holiday trip, and it has come and gone since.
Doctor: Any chest pain, fainting, or shortness of breath at rest?
Patient: No chest pain, and I haven't passed out. I get a little short of breath climbing stairs, and I feel lightheaded and tired when it races.
Doctor: Any weakness on one side, trouble speaking, or vision changes?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any bleeding problems?
Patient: No bleeding problems.
Doctor: What do you drink? Caffeine, alcohol?
Patient: Two or three energy drinks a day for work, and wine on weekends.
Doctor: Do you take any cold medicines or decongestants?
Patient: I've been taking pseudoephedrine for my sinuses most days for the last month.
Doctor: That can trigger fast rhythms, so I'd like you to stop it. Now, let's review your medicines and allergies.
Patient: I'm allergic to aspirin and ibuprofen. They give me hives.
Doctor: Thank you. That matters because we will avoid aspirin and all anti-inflammatory pain pills. What else do you take?
Patient: Levothyroxine 100 mcg every morning for my thyroid, and losartan 25 mg... no wait, I have the bottle here, it's 50 mg once a day for my blood pressure. And the metoprolol since the ER. I use acetaminophen for headaches.
Doctor: Good. Any chance you could be pregnant?
Patient: No, I have an IUD.
Doctor: Okay. Now your results. The ECG in the ER and the one we did today both show atrial fibrillation. Today your ventricular rate is 112 and there are no ST changes. Blood pressure is 142/90, heart rate 112 and irregular, and oxygen saturation 98 percent. Your TSH was 1.8, hemoglobin 13.4, creatinine 0.8, and potassium 4.1. Your echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 58 percent with mild left atrial enlargement and no significant valve disease. On exam, the rhythm is irregular, there is no murmur, your lungs are clear, and there is no leg swelling.
Doctor: So this is newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation, likely triggered by the energy drinks and pseudoephedrine, with your hypertension contributing. Your stroke risk score is 2 because you are female and have hypertension, so I recommend a blood thinner. With your aspirin allergy we would not use aspirin anyway, so I'll start apixaban 5 mg twice daily. I'll also increase metoprolol succinate from 25 mg to 50 mg once daily for rate control, and I'm stopping the pseudoephedrine. Please stop the energy drinks and limit the wine. Avoid ibuprofen and keep using acetaminophen for headaches. I'll order a sleep study because you snore and feel tired. Come back in two weeks for a repeat ECG, and go to the ER for chest pain, fainting, or stroke symptoms like a drooping face or trouble speaking.
Patient: Okay. Is this permanent?
Doctor: Not necessarily. If it persists, we can talk about cardioversion or ablation later.
Patient: Okay, I understand.

Doctor: Good to see you. You're an 84-year-old male here for your routine HIV follow-up. How have you been since last time?
Patient: Not too bad. A bit tired, but I'm old, so that's expected.
Doctor: Any fevers, night sweats, weight loss, cough, or diarrhea?
Patient: No fevers, no night sweats, and my weight is steady. No cough, no diarrhea.
Doctor: How is your sleep?
Patient: I wake up a lot at night. No falls, though.
Doctor: Tell me about your medicines. Are you taking your HIV pills every day?
Patient: Yes, Biktarvy, one tablet once a day with breakfast. I haven't missed any that I can think of. Maybe two this month, when I had a rough night.
Doctor: And your other medications?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg a day for my blood pressure. That's all.
Doctor: Let's talk about drinking. How much alcohol do you have in a typical day?
Patient: A few beers. Maybe six, sometimes eight, in the evening. It got worse after my wife passed.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. That is heavy alcohol use, and it matters for your liver and your sleep, and it can lead to missed pills. Any shakes in the morning or seizures when you skip a drink?
Patient: My hands shake a little in the morning until I have my first beer. No seizures.
Doctor: Any vomiting blood, black stools, or belly pain?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Your blood pressure today is 136/78, so your hypertension is reasonably controlled, and your heart rate is 74. Your weight is stable. You are alert, there is a mild fine tremor of both hands, your abdomen is soft and nontender, and I don't feel an enlarged liver. Your labs from last week show your HIV viral load is undetectable and your CD4 count is 540. ALT is 58 and AST is 72, which are mildly elevated. Hemoglobin is 12.8 and creatinine is 1.1.
Doctor: The good news is that your HIV is well controlled. The liver tests are probably from the alcohol. I want you to cut down gradually rather than stopping suddenly, because stopping all at once can be dangerous at your level of drinking. Starting today, I'm adding thiamine 100 mg once a day and folic acid 1 mg once a day. Continue Biktarvy one tablet daily and amlodipine as you are taking them. I'll refer you to our addiction counselor, and we can talk about a medicine to reduce cravings next visit after we recheck your liver tests. We'll repeat the liver tests and viral load in three months.
Patient: Okay, I'll try.
Doctor: Come back in three months, or sooner if you have more shaking, confusion, or black stools.

The assessment is well-controlled HIV with heavy alcohol use and probable alcohol-related liver test elevation. The plan is to cut down gradually, start thiamine and folic acid, continue Biktarvy and amlodipine, refer to an addiction counselor, and repeat liver tests and viral load in three months.

History per mother: This 9-year-old female has had two days of sore throat, pain with swallowing, and fever up to a temperature of 38.6 C this morning on an oral thermometer at home. She has had no cough, runny nose, ear pain, rash, vomiting, or trouble breathing, and no drooling. She is eating less but drinking fluids and urinating normally. A brother had strep throat last month.

The rapid strep test was done yesterday at an urgent care and was positive, as read by the mother from the paperwork. No throat culture was sent.

Past medical history includes asthma, eczema, and allergic rhinitis. Medications reviewed with the mother by phone: fluticasone 44 mcg, two puffs twice daily with a spacer; albuterol inhaler, 2 puffs as needed, last used two weeks ago; and cetirizine 10 mg once daily, which the allergist raised from 5 mg a month ago. Home observations: temperature 38.6 C, comfortable breathing per mother, speaking in full sentences on the phone, no wheezing heard. Asthma has been quiet with no night symptoms this week.

My impression is streptococcal pharyngitis, confirmed by a positive rapid strep test, in a child with well controlled asthma, eczema, and allergic rhinitis. The history is typical, with fever, tonsillar exudate, and no cough or runny nose.

Recommendations: Start amoxicillin 1000 mg by mouth once daily for 10 days, sent to the pharmacy. For fever or throat pain, acetaminophen 450 mg every 6 hours as needed, or ibuprofen 200 mg every 6 hours as needed with food, no more than 4 doses a day of either. Encourage fluids, soft foods, and salt water gargles. Continue fluticasone, albuterol as needed, and cetirizine; do not restart montelukast. She may return to school after 12 hours of antibiotics once she has no fever. Replace her toothbrush after 2 days of antibiotics and complete the full 10 days. A test of cure is not needed. Call or go to the emergency department for trouble breathing, drooling, inability to swallow fluids, stiff neck, severe ear pain, a new rash, or neck swelling, and call in the next few weeks for dark urine or facial swelling. The mother repeated the dosing back correctly. Nurse phone check in 3 days, with an in-person visit if she is not improving within 48 hours.

summary: A 45-year-old female with limited health literacy presented to the ED asking for help to quit drinking after about eight years of daily alcohol use. She received lorazepam and thiamine, improved, and was transferred to an inpatient detox unit.
